title: Budj Bim eel traps and Cultural Landscape
summary: At Budj Bim in south-west Victoria the Gunditjmara used channels, weirs and dams built on lava flows to trap, store and harvest kooyang, the short-finned eel. The Budj Bim site states they created and managed this system for at least 6,600 years, and describes "deep time" as the idea that they have always been there. The landscape was inscribed on the World Heritage List in August 2019.

uncertainty.note: Start is approximate: sources say "at least 6,600 years" (Budj Bim site) and charcoal "carbon-dated to 6,600 years old" (Australian National Maritime Museum), counted back from the present and rounded to -4600; no calibrated range was given. End is the August 2019 World Heritage inscription.

reviewer_note: UNESCO (whc.unesco.org/en/list/1577), Parks Victoria and DJPR pages returned 403, so the listing month comes only from the budjbim.com.au page, which that page itself draws from the UNESCO listing; please confirm against UNESCO. The Gunditjmara wording ("deep time", native title recognised 2007) is from budjbim.com.au; the publisher relationship to Gunditj Mirring Traditional Owners Aboriginal Corporation was not verified from an opened page (the sites page says GMTOAC owns and manages several sites). The sea.museum page says the Muldoons charcoal is 6,600 years old and gives "around 6,000 years" for the start of the eel farms. Coordinate is the OSM peak/volcano point; the landscape spans about 35 km (sea.museum).
